tsh.origin: The 0.4 to 4.5 mIU/L group of reference intervals derives from NHANES III (1988 to 1994): of 17,353 United States residents aged 12 years and over, 16,533 were “disease-free” and 13,344 formed a “reference population” after exclusion of pregnancy, hormone use, positive thyroid antibodies and biochemical dysfunction [S3]. The disease-free upper reference limit was 4.5 mIU/L and the reference-population interval 0.45 to 4.12 mIU/L, as stated in the 2012 guideline of the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and the American Thyroid Association [S4]. No interval was derived separately for women, although TSH was higher and antibody positivity more common in women [S3].
tsh.sexSpecificWhat: Pregnancy only: the American Thyroid Association 2017 upper reference limit is approximately 4.0 mU/L (about 0.5 mU/L below the non-pregnant limit) from weeks 7 to 12 where no local trimester-specific interval exists; no laboratory or guideline consulted gives a sex-specific interval for non-pregnant adults. By age, the 97.5th centile was 3.56 mIU/L at 20 to 29 years and 7.49 mIU/L at 80 years and over.
tsh.contestedSummary: The upper reference limit “has not been universally accepted”: proposals of 2.5 or 3.0 mIU/L rest on the right skew of the reference distribution (values of 3.1 to 4.12 mIU/L) and a median near 1.5 mIU/L [S4]; the 2003 “0.3-3.0” proposal of the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists is reported in secondary sources only [S10]. Opponents of these proposals note that 85% of the NHANES III reference group had TSH below 2.5 mIU/L and that lowering the limit would add “more than 10 million additional diagnoses” per year [S4, S5]. A 2019 BMJ guideline (21 trials, 2,192 participants) recommends strongly against treating subclinical hypothyroidism, except for women planning pregnancy, patients with TSH above 20 mIU/L or severe symptoms, and young adults [S12].
tsh.guidanceInBand: Recommendation 16 of the 2012 guideline of the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and the American Thyroid Association (ATA) states: “Treatment based on individual factors for patients with TSH levels between the upper limit of a given laboratory's reference range and 10 mIU/L should be considered particularly if patients have symptoms suggestive of hypothyroidism, positive TPOAb or evidence of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease” [S4]; for TSH of 2.5 to 4.5 mIU/L, “there are virtually no clinical outcome data to support treating” [S4]. In pregnancy, Recommendation 29 of the ATA 2017 guideline states that levothyroxine “may be considered” for thyroid peroxidase antibody (TPOAb)-positive women with TSH above 2.5 mU/L and below the upper limit of the pregnancy interval, and is “not recommended” for TPOAb-negative women with TSH within the pregnancy interval “or < 4.0 mU/L if unavailable” [S6].
tsh.labRangeSource: LabCorp test 004259 (above 10 years, ECLIA); ARUP test 0070145 reports 0.27 to 4.20 mU/L at 20 years and over.

S10.title: TSH Range Is Not Universally Applicable
S10.note: Secondary report of the AACE 2003 proposal of 0.3 to 3.0.

ft4.origin: The interval is from a manufacturer (Roche Elecsys) reference-interval study cited by the laboratory, whose page does not describe the population [S1]. The study itself was not verified.
ft4.sexSpecificWhat: Pregnancy only: Recommendation 2 of the American Thyroid Association 2017 guideline requires “assay method-specific and trimester-specific pregnancy reference ranges” because analogue free T4 immunoassays are “influenced by pregnancy” [S3]. There is no sex-specific non-pregnant interval.
ft4.contestedSummary: Indirect analogue free T4 immunoassays vary “significantly by manufacturer” and are affected by pregnancy; the reference method (equilibrium dialysis LC-MS/MS) is “not widely available” [S3].
ft4.guidanceInBand: Recommendation 30 of the American Thyroid Association 2017 guideline states: “Isolated hypothyroxinemia should not be routinely treated in pregnancy. (Weak recommendation, Low quality evidence)” [S3].

vitamin_d.origin: The laboratory categories reproduce the Endocrine Society 2011 scheme: deficiency “below 20 ng/ml”, insufficiency “21-29 ng/ml” and sufficiency “30-100 ng/ml” [S3]. The Institute of Medicine (IOM) 2011 Dietary Reference Intakes report, from the same bone data, set 16 ng/mL (40 nmol/L) as the average requirement and 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) as the concentration at which “Practically all persons are sufficient” [S2]. Neither threshold was derived by sex; the IOM Estimated Average Requirement and Recommended Dietary Allowance for vitamin D are the same for men and women [S2].
vitamin_d.sexSpecificWhat: No sex-specific 25(OH)D threshold appears in the Institute of Medicine 2011, Endocrine Society 2011 or 2024, US Preventive Services Task Force 2021 or UK Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition 2016 documents. The Endocrine Society 2024 guideline suggests empiric supplementation in pregnancy without a threshold [S4].
vitamin_d.contestedSummary: Institute of Medicine (IOM) committee members responded in 2012 to “aspects of The Endocrine Society guideline that are not well supported” [S6]; the Endocrine Society 2024 guideline “no longer endorses the target 25(OH)D level of 30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L)” and no longer endorses “specific 25(OH)D levels to define vitamin D sufficiency” [S4]. The IOM value of 20 ng/mL is a population coverage value (97.5% of people), not an individual decision threshold, with the average requirement at 16 ng/mL [S2]. The US Preventive Services Task Force (2021) states that “no one serum vitamin D level cutpoint defines deficiency” and that evidence for screening is insufficient [S9]. The UK Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition uses 25 nmol/L (10 ng/mL) as a population protective level and states that it “is not a clinical threshold diagnostic of the disease” [S7].
vitamin_d.guidanceInBand: The Endocrine Society 2011 guideline defines “vitamin D insufficiency as a 25(OH)D of 21-29 ng/ml” [S3]. The Institute of Medicine 2011 report states: “Practically all persons are sufficient at serum 25OHD levels of at least 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL)” [S2]. The Endocrine Society 2024 guideline states: “In healthy adults, we suggest against routine screening for 25(OH)D levels”; it “suggests against empiric vitamin D supplementation above the current DRI” (Dietary Reference Intake) for adults under 75 years, while suggesting empiric supplementation at 75 years and over and “during pregnancy” [S4].
vitamin_d.labRangeSource: ARUP test 2002348 (LC-MS/MS, adults 18 years and over): “Optimum level 30-80 ng/mL”; deficiency below 20 ng/mL; insufficiency 20 to 29 ng/mL.

S8.title: Vitamin D Deficiency - Is There Really a Pandemic?
S8.note: Bibliographic record only; full text not consulted.

testosterone_female.origin: The laboratory pages do not state the population underlying the female interval. Published female reference intervals derive from Haring et al. (2012), using LC-MS/MS in 985 women aged 20 to 80 from one German cohort (2.5th to 97.5th percentile 0.35 to 1.97 nmol/L, about 10 to 57 ng/dL, declining with age) [S3], and Braunstein et al. (2011), using immunoassay in 161 normally cycling women aged 18 to 49 (5th to 95th percentile 15 to 46 ng/dL at age 30 years) [S4]. The Endocrine Society 2007 assay statement calls for normative values “for both genders and children” to be established only after assay standardisation [S7].
testosterone_female.sexSpecificWhat: Lower reference limit of the adult reference interval by sex (ARUP, LC-MS/MS). No guideline defines a threshold for “low testosterone” in women: “No cutoff blood level can be used for any measured circulating androgen to differentiate women with and without sexual dysfunction” [S6].
testosterone_female.contestedSummary: A global consensus statement holds that “Direct assays for the measurement of total and free testosterone are highly unreliable in the female range” (Grade A), whereas LC-MS/MS measures “with high accuracy and reproducibility” [S6]. The LabCorp female interval is produced on a direct electrochemiluminescence immunoassay [S2], and ARUP reports no female interval for its immunoassay [S1b]. The published reference intervals rest on 985 women [S3] and 161 women [S4]. The Endocrine Society 2014 guideline states: “We recommend against making a clinical diagnosis of androgen deficiency syndrome in healthy women”, citing “a lack of a well-defined syndrome” and “the lack of valid reference ranges for women” [S5].
testosterone_female.guidanceInBand: A global consensus statement holds that “A blood total testosterone level should not be used to diagnose HSDD” (hypoactive sexual desire disorder) [S6]. The Endocrine Society states: “We recommend against making a clinical diagnosis of androgen deficiency syndrome in healthy women” [S5]. Where testosterone is prescribed, “Dosing should be limited to achieving testosterone concentrations in the physiologic premenopausal range” [S6].
testosterone_female.labRangeSource: ARUP test 0081058 (LC-MS/MS): premenopausal women 18 years and over 9 to 55 ng/dL; postmenopausal women 5 to 32 ng/dL; men 18 to 39 years 300 to 1080 ng/dL. LabCorp test 004226 (ECLIA): women 20 to 30 years 13 to 71; 31 to 40 years 8 to 60; 41 to 60 years 4 to 50 ng/dL.

amh.origin: The laboratory pages report age-banded percentiles without naming the population; the lower reference limits of the two laboratories for women aged 30 to 35 differ about fourfold (0.66 and 0.176 ng/mL) [S1, S2]. Values are method-specific because no international standard existed: in the 2020 study by the WHO and the National Institute for Biological Standards and Control, the candidate reagent 16/190 was commutable for 6 methods, partially commutable for 3 and non-commutable for 7 of 16 valid methods, and the WHO established it as a Reference Reagent only [S3].
amh.sexSpecificWhat: Reference intervals are female-specific and age-specific by construction; no guideline defines a fertility threshold. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists states that a single AMH measurement “should not be used for counseling patients in this regard” (time to pregnancy) outside infertility care [S4].
amh.contestedSummary: Steiner et al. (2017) studied 750 women aged 30 to 44 with no history of infertility: at AMH below 0.7 ng/mL (n = 84) and at 0.7 to 8.4 ng/mL, the probability of conception was, respectively, 65% (95% CI 50 to 75) and 62% (57 to 66) by 6 cycles and 84% (70 to 91) and 75% (70 to 79) by 12 cycles; the adjusted hazard ratio was 1.19 (0.88 to 1.61). Low AMH values “were not associated with reduced fertility” [S6]. Laboratories nonetheless flag low-for-age values, and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists issued an opinion addressing women “not seeking fertility care” [S4]; 7 of 16 assay methods are non-commutable with the WHO reagent [S3].
amh.guidanceInBand: Committee Opinion 773 of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists states that AMH “should not be used for counseling patients in this regard” (time to pregnancy) and that routine testing to predict pregnancy loss “is not recommended” [S4]. The American Society for Reproductive Medicine (2020) states that ovarian-reserve markers “are weak predictors of reproductive potential when age is taken into account” [S5].
amh.labRangeSource: LabCorp test 500183 (electrochemiluminescence), women: 20 to 25 years 1.23 to 11.51; 26 to 30 years 1.03 to 11.10; 31 to 35 years 0.66 to 8.75; 36 to 40 years 0.42 to 8.34; 41 to 46 years 0.26 to 5.81; 47 to 54 years ≤0.82; 55 years and over ≤0.18 ng/mL. ARUP test 2002656 (ELISA): 18 to 29 years 0.401 to 16.015; 30 to 39 years 0.176 to 11.705; 40 to 45 years ≤6.282 ng/mL.

prolactin.origin: The intervals derive from manufacturer reference-interval studies (LabCorp cites the Roche package insert) [S2]; the population is not described. The Endocrine Society 2011 guideline states: “Assay-specific normal values are higher in women than in men and are generally lower than 25 μg/liter” [S3].
prolactin.sexSpecificWhat: Upper reference limit of the adult reference interval (ARUP). ARUP also reports 9.7 to >200 ng/mL in pregnancy and 1.8 to 20.3 ng/mL in postmenopausal women [S1].
prolactin.contestedSummary: Macroprolactin, a biologically inactive prolactin-IgG complex, is detected by immunoassays: “All prolactin assays currently available are affected with 5-25% of results” indicating hyperprolactinaemia being falsely elevated [S4]. Suliman et al. (2003) identified 21 women in whom hyperprolactinaemia (above 1000 mIU/L) was “accounted for entirely by the presence of macroprolactin”; pituitary imaging had been performed in 93% and dopamine agonists prescribed in 87% [S5].
prolactin.guidanceInBand: Recommendation 1.1 of the Endocrine Society 2011 guideline states that “a level above the upper limit of normal confirms the diagnosis as long as the serum sample was obtained without excessive venipuncture stress”; Recommendation 1.2 states: “In patients with asymptomatic hyperprolactinemia, we suggest assessing for macroprolactin” [S3].
prolactin.labRangeSource: ARUP test 0070115 (chemiluminescent immunoassay, 10 years and over); LabCorp test 004465 reports female 13 to 50 years 4.8 to 33.4 ng/mL and male 31 to 50 years 3.9 to 22.7 ng/mL.

vitamin_b12.origin: The interval is that of the manufacturer. The historical decision threshold, “commonly set in the region of 200 ng/L (148 pmol/L)”, derives partly from older radioassay and microbiological methods rather than current assays [S3]; the British Society for Haematology 2014 guideline states that thresholds cannot be standardised across methods and recommends local reference intervals [S4].
vitamin_b12.sexSpecificWhat: No sex-specific threshold was identified; pregnancy is treated as an interpretive exception, without a verified numeric threshold [S3].
vitamin_b12.contestedSummary: Harrington et al. state: “There is no gold standard test for deficiency” [S3]. National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guideline NG239 (2024) “suggests an indeterminate range of 180 to 350 ng/L (133 to 258 pmol/L)”, with methylmalonic acid measurement for symptomatic people [S3]; a UK survey found that 16.6% of laboratories used the NG239 threshold of 180 ng/L and that reported thresholds ranged from 65 to 239 ng/L [S5]. The LabCorp lower reference limit (232 pg/mL) falls within that indeterminate range [S1].
vitamin_b12.guidanceInBand: Guideline NG239, as described by Harrington et al. (2025), states: “MMA measurement should be considered in people who have symptoms or signs of B12 deficiency” (MMA: methylmalonic acid) [S3]. The British Society for Haematology 2014 guideline states that treatment should not be delayed when clinical features strongly suggest deficiency but test results disagree [S4].
